paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disease that appears within the first weeks of life. It is characterized by a selective failure to absorb dietary glucose and galactose from the intestine. The resulting severe diarrhea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991; Martin et al., 1996). The disorder is caused by a defect in SGLT1, the Na+/glucose cotransporter of the intestinal brush border (Martin et al., 1996).

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) studied glucose transport by jejunal mucosa in vitro and by kidney in vivo in an affected girl, her family, and 16 normal volunteers. In normal human jejunal mucosa, glucose transport was concentrative, saturable, sodium and energy dependent, and showed competitive inhibition. Biopsy specimens from 6 normal controls and from the proband's asymptomatic brother accumulated glucose to 16 times the concentration in the incubation medium. In contrast, the proband's mucosa could not concentrate glucose at any point during a 60-minute incubation. Both parents and a half sister had impaired glucose transport, with values between those of normal subjects and the proband. In these 3 heterozygotes, glucose influx was impaired but glucose efflux was the same as in normal controls. Kinetic analysis showed a reduced capacity (Vmax) with a normal affinity (Km) for glucose transport. All subjects accumulated fructose similarly. Renal glucose titration showed a partial defect in renal glucose reabsorption in the proband, whereas her brother's titration curve was similar to those of 7 normal volunteers.

paragraphs.text: In a family with glucose/galactose malabsorption, Turk et al. (1991) found a single missense mutation in the SGLT1 gene that cosegregated with the disease. Xenopus oocytes injected with the mutant cRNA completely lost Na(+)-dependent glucose transport. Turk et al. (1993) stated that this mutation, found in 2 patients with GGM, was an asp28-to-asn (D28N) substitution and that it abolished SGLT1 transport activity in vitro.
